decks.title: Biodiversity and its Conservation — Part 1: Biodiversity and its patterns
goals: Distinguish genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, and state the global numbers and proportions of major taxa
Explain the latitudinal gradient and the species–area relationship (graph and equation)
Explain the rivet popper hypothesis and the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons for conserving biodiversity

slides.heading: Biodiversity
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what biodiversity is, how it is distributed, and why it matters.

visual.alt: Flow from genetic diversity to species diversity to ecosystem diversity

slides.narration: Biodiversity, a term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson, is the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation, from genes to whole ecosystems.

slides.heading: Three levels of biodiversity
slides.body_md: Biodiversity exists at three levels.

rows: Rauwolfia vomitoria in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency of its chemical reserpine; India has over 50 000 strains of rice and about 1000 varieties of mango
The Western Ghats have a greater diversity of amphibian species than the Eastern Ghats
India’s deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, far more than a Scandinavian country

visual.alt: Table of the three levels of biodiversity

slides.narration: A single medicinal plant may differ in its chemistry from one mountain range to another. The number of species differs from region to region. And a large country with varied landscapes holds many different kinds of ecosystem.

slides.heading: How many species are there?
slides.body_md: The **IUCN (2004)** puts the number of described species at slightly more than **1.5 million**; **Robert May** estimated the global total at about **7 million**. More than **70 percent** of recorded species are **animals**; plants are no more than **22 percent**; among animals, **insects** are more than 70 percent.

slides.heading: India’s biodiversity
slides.body_md: India has only **2.4 percent** of the world’s land area but about **8.1 percent** of global species diversity, making it one of the **12 mega-diversity countries**.

rows: About twice as many as plants

visual.alt: Table of approximate species numbers in India

slides.narration: India holds more than three times its share of the world’s species, considering its land area. Many of its species, and many of the world’s, are yet to be discovered and named.

slides.narration: The tropics hold far more species than temperate or polar regions. A tropical forest like the Amazon has tens of thousands of plant species, thousands of fish, and over a thousand bird species.

slides.heading: Why are the tropics so diverse?
slides.body_md: Ecologists have proposed several reasons.

rows: Tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years, allowing long evolutionary time for speciation
Less seasonal, more constant and predictable conditions promote niche specialisation
More solar energy contributes to higher productivity, which can support more species

visual.alt: Table of reasons for high tropical diversity

slides.narration: Temperate regions were repeatedly glaciated in the past, while the tropics were not. Their steady climate and abundant energy allow many species to specialise and coexist.

slides.heading: Quick check: genetic diversity
slides.body_md: Variation in reserpine content of Rauwolfia from different Himalayan ranges is an example of which level of biodiversity?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is it about genes, species or ecosystems?

slides.heading: The species–area relationship
slides.body_md: **Alexander von Humboldt** observed that within a region, **species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit**. On a normal scale the relation is a **rectangular hyperbola**; on a log scale it is a **straight line**: **log S = log C + Z log A**, or **S = CA^Z**, where S is species richness, A area, C the Y-intercept and Z the slope.

visual.alt: Species–area curve and its straight-line log–log form

slides.narration: Z, the slope or regression coefficient, is usually between point one and point two for any taxonomic group or region. But when very large areas such as whole continents are compared, the slope is much steeper, from about point six to one point two.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using S = CA^Z
slides.body_md: (i) With Z = 0.25, by what factor does the number of species rise if the area surveyed is made 16 times larger? (ii) With C = 12 and Z = 0.25, how many species are expected in an area of 625 km²?
bullets: (i) Factor $= 16^{0.25} = 2$: species double.
(ii) $S = 12 \times 625^{0.25} = 12 \times 5 = 60$ species.

visual.alt: Worked table: species double; 60 species

slides.narration: Because Z is small, even a big increase in area gives only a modest increase in species: sixteen times the area merely doubles them. The same equation predicts how many species a given area should hold.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding Z from two surveys
slides.body_md: A survey found 50 species of beetles in 100 km² and 200 species in 10 000 km² of the same region. Find Z.
bullets: $Z = \dfrac{\log S_{2} - \log S_{1}}{\log A_{2} - \log A_{1}} = \dfrac{\log 200 - \log 50}{\log 10000 - \log 100}$.

visual.alt: Worked table: Z about 0.3

slides.narration: Taking logarithms turns the curve into a straight line whose slope is Z. Here Z is about point three, a little above the usual range, as might happen when a larger, more varied area is compared.

slides.heading: Importance of species diversity: the rivet popper hypothesis
slides.body_md: **David Tilman** found that plots with **more species** showed **less year-to-year variation** in total biomass and higher productivity. **Paul Ehrlich’s rivet popper hypothesis** compares an ecosystem to an **aeroplane** and species to its **rivets**.

rows: A few rivets from seats or windows
Little immediate danger (loss of minor species)
A serious threat to the safety of the plane (loss of key species that drive major functions)

visual.alt: Table explaining the rivet popper hypothesis

slides.narration: Every species we lose weakens the ecosystem a little, and losing species that perform key functions is like pulling rivets from the wings. Richer communities also tend to be more stable and more productive.

slides.heading: Why should we conserve biodiversity?
slides.body_md: The reasons are grouped into three categories.

rows: Direct economic benefits: food, firewood, fibre, construction material, tannins, dyes, resins, perfumes; more than 25 percent of drugs come from plants; bioprospecting for useful products
Ecosystem services: the Amazon forest produces about 20 percent of the oxygen in the atmosphere through photosynthesis; pollination by bees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasure
Every species has an intrinsic value; we have a moral duty to care for it and pass it on to future generations

visual.alt: Table of reasons for conserving biodiversity

slides.narration: Some benefits are direct, like food and medicine. Others are services nature provides free, like clean air and pollination, which would be impossible to replace. And many people feel that every species has a right to exist.

slides.heading: Quick check: rivet popper
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the rivet popper hypothesis.
slides.narration: Quick check. In the analogy, what do the rivets stand for?

slides.heading: Quick check: tropics
slides.body_md: Which is a proposed reason for the high species diversity of the tropics?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about time, stability and energy.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Genetic (Rauwolfia, rice, mango), species (Western Ghats amphibians) and ecosystem diversity.
About 1.5 million species described (IUCN 2004); about 7 million estimated (May); over 70 percent animals, insects over 70 percent of animals.
India: 2.4 percent of land, 8.1 percent of species; one of 12 mega-diversity countries.
Latitudinal gradient; species–area relationship S = CA^Z (Humboldt), Z usually 0.1–0.2, 0.6–1.2 for continents.
Rivet popper hypothesis (Ehrlich); narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons for conservation.

visual.alt: Summary table of concepts and scientists

slides.narration: To recap: biodiversity exists at the level of genes, species and ecosystems, is richest in the tropics, rises with area according to a simple equation, and is worth conserving for practical, ecological and ethical reasons.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give an **Indian example** for each level of biodiversity.
Write **log S = log C + Z log A** and give the usual **values of Z**.
Quote **bird numbers** to illustrate the latitudinal gradient.
Explain the **rivet popper** analogy fully.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Use Indian examples for the three levels. Write the species–area equation in both forms and know the values of Z. Quote bird numbers for the latitudinal gradient. And explain the rivet popper analogy step by step.

decks.title: Biodiversity and its Conservation — Part 2: Loss and conservation of biodiversity
goals: Name recent extinctions and explain the four major causes of biodiversity loss
Describe in-situ conservation: biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves, hotspots, Ramsar sites and the Red Data Book
Describe ex-situ conservation, and the Earth Summit and World Summit

slides.heading: Loss and conservation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why species are disappearing, and how they can be protected.

visual.alt: Flow from loss of biodiversity to its causes and to in-situ, ex-situ and international conservation

slides.narration: The colonisation of islands by humans, and the spread of human activity everywhere, has led to the extinction of many species. Understanding why helps us decide how best to protect what remains.

slides.heading: Loss of biodiversity
slides.body_md: The **IUCN Red List (2004)** documents the extinction of **784 species** (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years.

rows: Three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian)

visual.alt: Table of recent extinctions

slides.narration: Today, more than fifteen thousand species face the threat of extinction, including about twelve percent of birds, twenty three percent of mammals and thirty two percent of amphibians. Loss of species reduces plant production and lowers resistance to disturbances.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the Red List
slides.body_md: Of the 784 species documented as extinct in the last 500 years, 338 were vertebrates. What percentage is this? Which group contributed the most extinctions?
bullets: Vertebrates $= \dfrac{338}{784} \times 100 = 43.1$ percent.
Invertebrates (359) contributed the **most**, followed by vertebrates (338) and plants (87).

visual.alt: Worked table: 43.1 percent vertebrates

slides.narration: Dividing each group by the total shows that vertebrates account for over forty percent of recorded extinctions, though invertebrates are the largest group. Many invertebrate extinctions are probably never recorded at all.

slides.heading: Causes: the evil quartet
slides.body_md: Four major causes drive the loss of biodiversity.

rows: Tropical rain forests once covered 14 percent of the land, now no more than 6 percent; the Amazon is cleared for soybeans and cattle
Steller’s sea cow and the passenger pigeon were hunted to extinction; many marine fish are over-harvested
Nile perch in Lake Victoria caused the extinction of over 200 species of cichlid fish; carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth; African catfish threatens native catfishes
When a host fish dies out, its specific parasites die too; a plant and its specialised pollinator

visual.alt: Table of the four causes of biodiversity loss

slides.narration: Habitat loss is the most important cause. Large fragments are needed by animals with big territories, and fragmentation also harms migratory animals. Introduced species can spread unchecked and wipe out native ones.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: shrinking rain forests
slides.body_md: Tropical rain forests once covered about 14 percent of the Earth’s land surface and now cover no more than 6 percent. What percentage of the original rain forest has been lost?
bullets: Loss $= \dfrac{14 - 6}{14} \times 100 = 57.1$ percent.
Since species richness rises with area, such losses mean the extinction of very many species.

visual.alt: Worked table: 57.1 percent of the rain forest lost

slides.narration: More than half of the original rain forest is gone. Using the species–area relationship, a large loss of area means a large loss of species, especially in the species-rich tropics.

slides.heading: Quick check: alien species
slides.body_md: What happened after Nile perch were introduced into Lake Victoria?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the native cichlid fish.

slides.heading: In-situ conservation: hotspots
slides.body_md: **In-situ** (on site) conservation protects species in their **natural habitats**. **Biodiversity hotspots** are regions with **very high species richness** and **high endemism**. There are **34** hotspots; three cover India: **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and the Himalaya**.

rows: Less than 2 percent of the Earth’s land
Could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 percent

visual.alt: Table about biodiversity hotspots

slides.narration: Protecting a few small regions with very many endemic species gives the greatest benefit for the effort. That is why conservation focuses on hotspots.

slides.heading: Protected areas and biosphere reserves
slides.body_md: India protects ecologically rich areas as **biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries**. A **biosphere reserve** has a strictly protected **core zone**, a **buffer zone** for limited activities, and a **transition zone** where people live and use resources sustainably.

slides.narration: National parks give strict protection to whole ecosystems; sanctuaries protect particular species while allowing some human activity; biosphere reserves protect large areas together with the local people who live there.

slides.heading: Sacred groves, Ramsar sites and the Red Data Book
slides.body_md: Other forms of in-situ protection and record-keeping.

rows: Forest tracts protected by tradition: Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas
Wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention (1971)
Kept by the IUCN; lists threatened species in categories such as extinct, critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable

visual.alt: Table of sacred groves, Ramsar sites and the Red Data Book

slides.narration: In sacred groves, all the trees and wildlife are venerated and protected, so they shelter many rare species. Ramsar sites protect wetlands, and the Red Data Book tells us which species most need help.

slides.heading: Quick check: hotspots
slides.body_md: Which region is one of the biodiversity hotspots covering India?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of a mountain range along India’s west coast.

slides.heading: Ex-situ conservation
slides.body_md: **Ex-situ** (off site) conservation protects threatened species **outside their natural habitat**.

rows: Zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks
Keep and breed threatened animals and plants
Breeds endangered animals for release into the wild
Stores gametes and embryos in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C for long periods
In vitro fertilisation and tissue culture
Produce offspring or plants from few individuals
Keep seeds of commercially important plants viable for long periods

visual.alt: Table of methods of ex-situ conservation

slides.narration: When a species is on the brink, its last individuals can be bred in captivity, and its gametes or seeds can be frozen for the future. Ex-situ methods are a back-up to protecting habitats, not a replacement.

slides.heading: International efforts
slides.body_md: Biodiversity knows no political boundaries, so conservation needs international action.

rows: Convention on Biological Diversity: conservation of biodiversity and sustainable use of its benefits
190 countries pledged to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss at global, regional and local levels

visual.alt: Table of the Earth Summit and the World Summit

slides.narration: At the Earth Summit, nations agreed to take measures for conserving biodiversity and using it sustainably. Ten years later, at the World Summit, they pledged to slow the rate of biodiversity loss.

slides.heading: Quick check: cryopreservation
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about cryopreservation.
slides.narration: Quick check. At what temperature are gametes stored?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Extinctions: dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller’s sea cow, three tiger subspecies; 784 in 500 years (IUCN 2004).
Evil quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien invasions (Nile perch, Parthenium, Lantana, water hyacinth, African catfish), co-extinctions.
In-situ: hotspots (34; three in India), biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves, Ramsar sites; Red Data Book.
Ex-situ: zoos, botanical gardens, safari parks, captive breeding, cryopreservation, seed banks, tissue culture.
Earth Summit (Rio, 1992) and World Summit (Johannesburg, 2002).

visual.alt: Summary table of in-situ and ex-situ conservation

slides.narration: To recap: species are being lost through habitat loss, over-exploitation, invasions and co-extinctions. We protect them in their natural homes, in zoos and seed banks, and through international agreements.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **evil quartet** with **one example** each.
Distinguish **in-situ and ex-situ** with examples.
Name **India’s three hotspots** and give the **Rio and Johannesburg** summits with years.
List **recent extinctions** with their locations.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the four causes with examples. Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation. Remember India’s hotspots and the two summits with their places and years. And name the recent extinctions.

notes.title: Biodiversity and its Conservation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Levels and extent of biodiversity
sections.body_md:
**Biodiversity** — a term popularised by the sociobiologist **Edward Wilson** — is the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.
- **Genetic diversity:** a single species may show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. The medicinal plant ***Rauwolfia vomitoria*** growing in different Himalayan ranges shows variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical **reserpine**. India has more than **50 000** genetically different strains of **rice** and about **1000** varieties of **mango**.
- **Species diversity:** diversity at the species level; for example the **Western Ghats** have a greater **amphibian** species diversity than the **Eastern Ghats**.
- **Ecological diversity:** at the ecosystem level; India, with its **deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows**, has a greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country such as Norway.

**How many species?** According to the **IUCN (2004)**, the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than **1.5 million**; **Robert May** placed the global species diversity at about **7 million**. More than **70 percent** of all recorded species are **animals**, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) are no more than **22 percent**. Among animals, **insects** are the most species-rich group, making up more than **70 percent** — out of every 10 animals, 7 are insects. The number of fungus species is more than that of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined.

**India** has only **2.4 percent** of the world’s land area, but its share of global species diversity is an impressive **8.1 percent**; it is one of the **12 mega-diversity countries**, with nearly **45 000** species of plants and twice as many of animals.

Variation in genes within a species.
One of 12 countries holding a very large share of the world’s species.

sections.heading: 2. Patterns of biodiversity and its importance
sections.body_md:
**Latitudinal gradients:** species diversity **decreases** as we move away from the **equator** towards the **poles**. Tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. **Colombia**, near the equator, has nearly **1400** species of birds, **New York** at 41° N has **105**, and **Greenland** at 71° N only **56**; **India**, largely in the tropics, has more than **1200**. A tropical forest such as the **Amazon** has the greatest biodiversity on Earth (more than 40 000 plant species, 3000 fishes, 1300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles and more than 125 000 invertebrates). Reasons proposed: (a) the tropics have remained relatively **undisturbed for millions of years**, giving long evolutionary time for diversification; (b) tropical environments are **less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable**, promoting **niche specialisation**; (c) there is **more solar energy**, contributing to **higher productivity**.

**Species–area relationship:** **Alexander von Humboldt** observed that within a region, **species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit**. On a normal scale the relation is a **rectangular hyperbola**; on a logarithmic scale it is a **straight line** described by
**log S = log C + Z log A** (S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient), C = Y-intercept), that is, **S = CA^Z**.
The value of **Z** lies in the range **0.1 to 0.2**, regardless of taxonomic group or region; for **very large areas** such as entire continents the slope is much steeper, **0.6 to 1.2** (for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, about 1.15).

**Importance of species diversity:** communities with more species tend to be **more stable** — **David Tilman’s** long-term experiments showed that plots with more species had **less year-to-year variation** in total biomass, and that increased diversity contributed to **higher productivity**. **Paul Ehrlich’s rivet popper hypothesis:** an ecosystem is like an **aeroplane** whose parts are joined by thousands of **rivets (species)**. Removing a few rivets from the seats or windows (loss of minor species) may not affect flight safety, but as more rivets are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak; loss of rivets on the **wings** (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is a **serious threat**.

**Why conserve biodiversity?**
- **Narrowly utilitarian:** humans derive countless **direct economic benefits** — food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicines; more than **25 percent** of drugs on the market are derived from plants; nations exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for economically important products practise **bioprospecting**.
- **Broadly utilitarian:** biodiversity provides **ecosystem services** — the **Amazon** forest is estimated to produce through photosynthesis about **20 percent** of the total oxygen in the Earth’s atmosphere; **pollination** by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasures.
- **Ethical:** every species has an **intrinsic value**, even if it has no economic value to us; we have a **moral duty** to care for its well-being and pass on our biological legacy to future generations.

sections.heading: 3. Loss of biodiversity
sections.body_md:
The colonisation of tropical Pacific islands by humans is said to have led to the extinction of more than 2000 species of native birds. The **IUCN Red List (2004)** documents the extinction of **784 species** (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. **Recent extinctions** include the **dodo** (Mauritius), **quagga** (Africa), **thylacine** (Australia), **Steller’s sea cow** (Russia) and **three subspecies of tiger** (**Bali, Javan, Caspian**); in the last twenty years alone, 27 species have disappeared. More than **15 500** species worldwide face the threat of extinction, including **12 percent of birds, 23 percent of mammals, 32 percent of amphibians and 31 percent of gymnosperms**. Loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to a **decline in plant production**, **lowered resistance** to environmental perturbations such as drought, and increased variability in ecosystem processes.

**Causes — the “evil quartet”:**
1. **Habitat loss and fragmentation** — the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than **14 percent** of the Earth’s land surface but now cover no more than **6 percent**; the **Amazon rain forest** (“lungs of the planet”) is being cut and cleared for cultivating **soya beans** or for conversion to grasslands for raising **beef cattle**. When large habitats are broken into small fragments, **mammals and birds** needing large territories and **migratory** animals are badly affected.
2. **Over-exploitation** — many species extinctions in the last 500 years (**Steller’s sea cow, passenger pigeon**) were due to over-exploitation by humans; many marine fish populations are over-harvested.
3. **Alien species invasions** — when alien species are introduced, some turn invasive and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species. The **Nile perch** introduced into **Lake Victoria** (East Africa) led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than **200 species of cichlid fish**. Invasive weeds such as **carrot grass (Parthenium)**, **Lantana** and **water hyacinth (Eichhornia)** threaten native species; the illegal introduction of the **African catfish *Clarias gariepinus*** for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes.
4. **Co-extinctions** — when a species becomes extinct, plant and animal species **obligately associated** with it also become extinct: when a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of **parasites** meets the same fate; co-evolved **plant–pollinator** mutualisms are another example.

sections.heading: 4. In-situ conservation
sections.body_md:
**In-situ (on site)** conservation protects species in their **natural habitat**, together with the whole ecosystem.

**Biodiversity hotspots** — regions with **very high levels of species richness** and **high degree of endemism** (species confined to that region). Initially 25 hotspots were identified; the number now stands at **34**. Three of them — **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and the Himalaya** — cover India’s exceptionally high biodiversity regions. Although all the hotspots together cover **less than 2 percent** of the Earth’s land area, they harbour an extremely high number of species; **strict protection** of these hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost **30 percent**.

**Protected areas** in India: ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as **biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries**. A **biosphere reserve** has a strictly protected **core zone**, a surrounding **buffer zone** where limited activities (research, education, tourism) are permitted, and an outer **transition zone** where people live and use resources sustainably. **National parks** protect whole ecosystems strictly; **sanctuaries** protect particular species while allowing some human activities.

**Sacred groves** — India has a history of religious and cultural traditions that emphasised protection of nature. In many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside, and all the trees and wildlife within them were venerated and given total protection. Such sacred groves are found in the **Khasi and Jaintia Hills** in Meghalaya, the **Aravalli Hills** of Rajasthan, the **Western Ghat** regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the **Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar** areas of Madhya Pradesh. In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.

**Ramsar sites** — wetlands of international importance designated under the **Ramsar Convention** (signed at Ramsar, Iran, in **1971**) for the conservation and wise use of wetlands.

**Red Data Book** — maintained by the **IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature)**, it documents threatened species and classifies them into categories such as **extinct, extinct in the wild, critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable**, guiding conservation priorities.

sections.heading: 5. Ex-situ conservation
sections.body_md:
**Ex-situ (off site)** conservation protects threatened animals and plants by taking them **out of their natural habitat** and placing them in special settings where they can be protected and given special care.
- **Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks** serve this purpose; many animals that have become extinct in the wild continue to be maintained in zoos.
- **Captive breeding** of endangered species, with release into the wild where possible.
- **Cryopreservation** — gametes of threatened species can be preserved in **viable and fertile condition for long periods** using cryopreservation techniques (storage in **liquid nitrogen at −196 °C**).
- **In vitro fertilisation** of eggs, and **tissue culture** methods for propagating plants.
- **Seed banks** — seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods.
Ex-situ methods complement, but cannot replace, the protection of natural habitats.

sections.heading: 6. International conventions
sections.body_md:
Biodiversity knows no political boundaries, and conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations.
- **The Earth Summit**, held in **Rio de Janeiro** in **1992**, called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for the **conservation of biodiversity** and the **sustainable utilisation of its benefits**; it produced the **Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)**, which also seeks fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
- **The World Summit on Sustainable Development**, held in **Johannesburg, South Africa**, in **2002**: **190 countries** pledged their commitment to achieve, **by 2010**, a **significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss** at global, regional and local levels.

- Writing Z as 0.6–1.2 for all regions (that is for whole continents; usually 0.1–0.2).

- Giving the Earth Summit as Johannesburg (Rio, 1992; Johannesburg was the World Summit, 2002).

questions.stem_md: What is the latitudinal gradient in species diversity? Give three reasons proposed to explain it.

answer.model_answer_md: Species diversity **decreases** from the **equator towards the poles** — for example, about 1400 bird species in Colombia but only 56 in Greenland. Reasons: (i) tropical latitudes have remained **undisturbed for millions of years**, giving long evolutionary time for **speciation**; (ii) tropical environments are **less seasonal, more constant and predictable**, promoting **niche specialisation**; (iii) more **solar energy** in the tropics gives **higher productivity**, supporting more species.

questions.stem_md: Describe the species–area relationship, giving its equation on a logarithmic scale and the usual values of Z, and explain what happens to the curve on a normal scale.

answer.model_answer_md: **Humboldt** found that species richness **increases with area**, but only **up to a limit**. On a **normal scale** the graph is a **rectangular hyperbola**, rising steeply and then levelling off. On a **log scale** it is a **straight line**: **log S = log C + Z log A** (S = species richness, A = area, C = Y-intercept, Z = slope). **Z** is usually **0.1–0.2**, but **0.6–1.2** when very large areas such as **whole continents** are compared.

questions.solution_md: Curve, equation, Z.

questions.stem_md: Explain the narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical arguments for conserving biodiversity, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Narrowly utilitarian:** biodiversity gives **direct economic benefits** — food, fibre, firewood, industrial products, and **medicines** (more than 25 percent of drugs come from plants). **Broadly utilitarian:** it provides **ecosystem services** — the **Amazon** produces about **20 percent** of atmospheric oxygen; bees and birds **pollinate** crops. **Ethical:** every species has **intrinsic value**, and we have a **moral duty** to protect it for future generations.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: According to the IUCN, about 12 percent of bird species, 23 percent of mammal species and 32 percent of amphibian species are threatened with extinction. Interpret these figures and suggest why amphibians might be the most threatened group.

answer.model_answer_md: **Amphibians** (32 percent) are the **most threatened**, followed by **mammals** (23 percent) and **birds** (12 percent). Amphibians live partly in **water and partly on land** and have **moist, permeable skins**, so they are very sensitive to **habitat loss**, especially draining of **wetlands**, to **pollution**, and to **disease**; many also have **small ranges**. Their decline is an early **warning** of environmental damage.
